Galley
GAL-ee
n. (a low vessel driven by oars; the warship of the ancient Mediterranean)
From Greek galea through Old French galie. The Authorized Version uses it once, in Isaiah's vision of a Jerusalem whose broad rivers no enemy warship can enter.

Biblical Definition

But there the glorious LORD will be unto us a place of broad rivers and streams; wherein shall go no galley with oars, neither shall gallant ship pass thereby. The picture is precise. Great rivers made cities rich and also made them reachable: the Tigris carried Assyria's ships and the Euphrates carried Babylon's. Isaiah promises Jerusalem the benefit without the exposure — broad waters that no war galley can navigate, because the river is the LORD himself. The chapter is full of the same exchange, the terrible scattering of the enemy and then the sight that replaces it: thine eyes shall see the king in his beauty; they shall behold the land that is very far off. And the centre of the passage is the great triple confession: for the LORD is our judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our king; he will save us. Judge, lawgiver, king — the whole civil order gathered into one Person, which is exactly the settlement Revelation reaches when John is shewn a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): a low flat-built vessel with one deck, navigated with sails and oars, used chiefly in the Mediterranean; in Scripture, the warship that cannot enter Zion's rivers.

expand to see more

GALLEY, n. A low flat-built vessel with one deck, navigated with sails and oars.

OAR, n. An instrument for rowing boats, being a piece of timber round or square at one end, and flat at the other.

GALLANT, a. Gay; well dressed; showy; splendid; magnificent.

LAWGIVER, n. One who makes or enacts a law; a legislator.

SECURITY, n. Freedom from danger; safety; freedom from fear or apprehension.

Key Scripture

Isa 33:21 — "But there the glorious LORD will be unto us a place of broad rivers and streams; wherein shall go no galley with oars, neither shall gallant ship pass thereby."

Isa 33:22 — "For the LORD is our judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our king; he will save us."

Isa 33:17 — "Thine eyes shall see the king in his beauty: they shall behold the land that is very far off."

Rev 22:1 — "And he shewed me a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb."

Modern Corruption

Security is sought in defences a people can build, and the offices of judge, lawgiver, and king are distributed among men as if they were ultimate; Isaiah gathers all three into the LORD and makes him the city's river.

expand to see more

Isaiah 33:22 is one of the great political verses of the Old Testament and it is not a manifesto for any human arrangement. The LORD is our judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our king. All three offices belong finally to One, which is why no human magistrate may claim any of them absolutely and why the dictionary holds that family, church, and state each hold delegated authority in their own sphere under Christ. A state that gathers all three to itself has claimed the verse for a creature.

The security promised is equally unlike anything a city could build. Not walls but water — broad rivers and streams that carry no enemy galley. Psalm 46 says it the same way: there is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God. Jerusalem had no river; that is the point. The safety of the people of God has never been a matter of defensible terrain, and the last picture Scripture gives of the city has a river in it flowing from the throne, with the nations healed by the leaves on its banks.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'oniy shayit (H590, H7885), a ship of oars; 'addiyr (H117), mighty or gallant; choqeq (H2710), a lawgiver.

Hebrew shayit (H7885) — an oar; with 'oniy, a galley with oars.

Hebrew 'addiyr (H117) — mighty, majestic, gallant; neither shall gallant ship pass thereby.

Hebrew shaphat (H8199) — to judge, to govern; the LORD is our judge.

Hebrew chaqaq (H2710) — to inscribe, to decree; the LORD is our lawgiver.

Hebrew yasha' (H3467) — to save, to deliver; he will save us.

Usage

"“wherein shall go no galley with oars” — the single occurrence."

"“the LORD is our judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our king” — the centre of the chapter."

"“Thine eyes shall see the king in his beauty” — what replaces the fear."
